nameStory: Borage gets its common name from the Arabic "abu rash," meaning "father of sweat," referring to its traditional use in folk medicine to induce sweating and break fevers. It's also called starflower because of its distinctive five-pointed, bright blue flowers that look like tiny stars scattered across the plant.
description: Borage is a cheerful annual herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with a sprawling, bushy habit. This Mediterranean native has become a beloved garden plant and occasional escape in New England. The plant is covered in coarse, bristly hairs and produces clusters of brilliant blue, star-shaped flowers that seem to glow against the gray-green foliage. Its cucumber-scented leaves and edible flowers make it a favorite among gardeners and pollinators alike.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright blue, five-petaled flowers arranged in perfect stars, about 3/4 inch across, with prominent black anthers in the center that form a cone shape

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval, gray-green leaves that smell distinctly like cucumber when crushed, covered in stiff, prickly hairs that feel rough and scratchy to touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling annual herb with hollow, succulent stems that branch freely and are covered in the same bristly hairs as the leaves

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels notably rough and bristly due to stiff white hairs covering stems, leaves, and even flower buds - almost sandpaper-like

habitat: In New England, borage is primarily found in herb gardens, vegetable plots, and occasionally as a garden escape in disturbed soils near cultivated areas. It prefers well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade and thrives in the loose, rich soil of gardens and compost areas.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring, producing rosettes of bristly, cucumber-scented leaves that are already quite rough to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant bright blue star flowers from June through August, attracting bees and other pollinators in large numbers.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering into early fall while simultaneously setting seed, with older plants becoming quite sprawling and bushy.
seasonality.winter: Annual plant dies with first hard frost, leaving behind seeds that may overwinter and germinate the following spring.

funFact: Borage flowers actually change color as they age - they start out pink in the bud, open to brilliant blue, and then fade to purple, meaning you can see three different colors on the same plant at once!
confusionNotes: The bright blue star-shaped flowers are quite distinctive, but young plants might be confused with comfrey, which is in the same family. However, comfrey has much larger, smoother leaves and bell-shaped flowers rather than star-shaped ones, plus it lacks borage's cucumber scent.
contextualKnowledge: While borage is generally considered safe and its flowers are popular as edible garnishes, the plant does contain small amounts of compounds that can be harmful in large quantities, so it should be consumed only in moderation as a culinary herb.
compareHints: Borage is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England gardens. Within the borage family, it's easily distinguished from relatives like comfrey and lungwort by its distinctive star-shaped blue flowers and strong cucumber scent. Most other borage family members have tubular or bell-shaped flowers rather than the flat, star-like blooms of true borage.
